subject: research/hanger-print
professional: a mechanical design engineer who designs FDM-printed load-bearing plastic parts (design for additive manufacturing); first checks: is the load case and bending axis right for the print orientation, are the material allowables sourced and matched to that orientation, is the off-axis (out-of-plane) and sustained-load (creep) case covered, and above all can the delivered file actually be sliced and printed on the stated printer

evidence.correctness: Recomputed independently of the package. Beam check by hand from Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials (sigma = Mc/I, cantilever tip delta = PL^3/3EI), script /tmp/.../scratchpad/hp/hand.py, no hanger_print import: rack w22 lever (220-28.6) cos 15.92 = 184.06 mm, sigma with Kt 2 and dynamic 2 = 0.8278 MPa, SF 48.32 (results.txt 48.32); w16 SF 70.39 and w25 41.77 (both match); static tip deflection w22 0.0233 mm, w25 0.0361 mm (results 0.023, 0.036); wire-like r 0.15 cm SF 0.130 and depth for SF 3 = 277.6 mm (README 0.13, 278); loop ligament tension 0.175 MPa (0.18). Independent STL reader (scratchpad/hp/stlcheck.py, parses the committed files, splits shells by shared vertices): every rack file is 5 closed, consistently oriented shells with 0 bad edges, z from 0 to 6.0 mm, and the minimal square footprint over 1-degree turns is 235.8 mm (w16), 276.7, 317.5, 358.3 mm (w25), all at 45 deg: confirms 'w16 fits a 256 bed, nothing fits 220 whole'. Errors found: the bed search steps in 5 degrees (geom.py:103), so the XXL (w 25.8) arm+hub actually fits 220 at 60.9 deg (219.3 mm) where results say 'no @60' (221.9 mm at 60); and the 'half' leaves out the post and loop that one half must carry (geom.py:99): with them the XXL half needs 225.3 mm. README.md:69 'each 25 cm arm is 150 cm^3' is 167.6 cm^3 at 12 mm (83.8 at 6 mm, STL). Numbers are right for the stated model; the model rests on assumed constants.
evidence.completeness: README claims: parametric STL for the four rack widths (present, closed meshes, checked above); OpenSCAD for the same (present, 5 linear_extrude per file, never rendered, stated); 'a stdlib Python generator and checker for any hanger-fit parameters' (library functions only; no CLI, run.py hard-codes the designs); strength, deflection, mass and bed checks (run, `PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py` reproduces results.txt). Not usable end to end: the only print files are whole hangers that the project's own result C says fit no 220 mm bed and only w16 fits 256, yet the owner steps (README.md:126,131) say print rack_w22.stl on 'any 220 mm bed'; w22 needs a 317.5 mm square. The two-piece split and joint, the shoulder profile and the adjustable mechanism are not designed (stated as next steps). Live page https://marisstella.app/research/hanger-print/ loads (HTTP 200) with the same summary.
evidence.verification: `/usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q` from the subject: 11 passed in 0.29 s (`python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` also OK). Six seeded mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: section modulus /6 -> /12 caught; bed search max -> min caught; lever without cos(slope) SURVIVED (the hand-calculation test uses slope 0); tip deflection 3EI -> 8EI SURVIVED (only a length-cubed ratio is tested, so the 0.04 mm headline is unpinned); loop ligament area x2 SURVIVED; sliced-mass walls halved SURVIVED. Mesh tests are good (closedness, orientation, volume = area x depth); the strength and mass outputs that the README reports are mostly unpinned.
evidence.craft: Read geom.py (111 lines), mesh.py (130), strength.py (79), run.py, test_print.py. Small, stdlib, readable, frozen dataclass, a real manifold check. Defects: bed search on an integer 5-degree grid gives wrong fit answers near the edge (geom.py:103); half-part excludes post and loop (geom.py:99); HUB_R defined and never used (geom.py:11); run.py:55 hard-codes hanger-fit's '1.6 mm' error as a string instead of reading it; sliced mass double-counts the overlapping shells (stated as an upper bound) and assumes 2 perimeters while the owner step prescribes 3; arm triangulation index maths in lambdas with no comment on the mirrored winding.
evidence.claims: Backed: every SF, depth and deflection figure in Results A and B (results.txt, recomputed); 'w16 fits 256 at 45 deg' (independent STL footprint); assumptions labelled and listed; limits section honest (no cloth, no creep, OpenSCAD unrendered, no joint); safety note. Not backed: title and headline answer 'does it hold a garment? Yes' (README.md:4) for a part never printed or loaded, with assumed constants; 'each 25 cm arm is 150 cm^3' (README.md:69; 167.6 at 12 mm); 'not for the 25.8 cm XXL' (README.md:92) is a 5-degree-grid artefact for arm+hub and right only once the post is included; owner step 'Print rack_w22.stl ... a printer (any 220 mm bed)' (README.md:126,131) contradicts result C; 'about 100 g of filament' vs the model's 83 g for w22. Material constants are called 'typical datasheet value' (strength.py:13) with no datasheet cited, though PLA technical data sheets are public; the page labels the project 'Stylised', which research/CLAUDE.md asks runs to avoid when the real figure is findable.
evidence.fitness: Job walked through as a maker or robot builder: take rack_w22.stl to a slicer for a 220 or 256 mm printer: it does not fit (317.5 mm square needed), and there is no split file or joint, so the deliverable cannot be printed on the printer the README names. As a researcher: the generator is reusable and the strong-axis beam check is a sound first pass, but the findings are textbook consequences (bending stress scales as 1/t^2, so a 3 mm arm is 360 times more stressed than a 57 mm one; a 43 cm hanger does not fit a 22 cm bed). Nearest prior work: the many parametric and split clothes-hanger designs on Printables and Thingiverse (OpenSCAD customizer hangers, two-piece dovetail hangers made for 220 mm beds) and standard DfAM practice; nothing here is new, and it is a milestone by-product, not a step toward the PhD-level paper research/CLAUDE.md sets as the bar.
evidence.domain: Against standard plastic-part beam design (Gere & Goodno; Roark for the cantilever): the load case (half the garment at the tip, dynamic factor 2), the strong-axis section 2r by depth and the in-plane (along-layer) allowable for a flat print are right and conservative. Departures, none of which changes the conclusion: no out-of-plane or torsion check, the weak axis at the 6 mm STL depth (my check: 20% of the tip load sideways gives sigma 3.2 MPa, SF 12.7 for w22); Euler-Bernoulli at span/depth about 3.2 (Timoshenko shear adds about 8% to deflection, 0.0018 of 0.0233 mm); creep named but not quantified although nominal static stress is about 0.2 MPa, far below PLA creep concern; loop as net-section tension with no pin-loaded-lug factor (Peterson); E 3500 MPa and 40 MPa allowable uncited (printed PLA tensile modulus is commonly nearer 2.3-3.0 GPa on vendor sheets, from my knowledge, not fetched). A DfAM engineer would sign off the strength check, not the print files, because the split is the real design problem and it is absent.

defects.what: The only print files are whole hangers that the project's own result C says fit no 220 mm bed (rack_w22.stl needs a 317.5 mm square), yet the owner steps say to print rack_w22.stl on 'any 220 mm bed'; no split file or joint exists, so the deliverable cannot be printed on the printer named

Bed-fit search uses an integer 5-degree grid and the 'half' omits the post and loop one half must carry: XXL arm+hub reported 221.9 mm (no) though it fits at 60.9 deg (219.3 mm); with the post and loop it needs 225.3 mm, so the README's conclusion is right only by accident
Headline answers 'does it hold a garment?' with 'Yes' though no part was printed or loaded and every material constant is assumed

Four of six seeded mutants survive: the lever's cos(slope), the deflection constant behind the 0.04 mm headline, the loop ligament area and the sliced-mass walls are not pinned by any test (the hand-calculation test uses slope 0)
PLA modulus 3500 MPa and 40 MPa allowable are called 'typical datasheet value' with no datasheet cited, though vendor technical data sheets are public; the page labels the work 'Stylised'
'each 25 cm arm is 150 cm^3 before slicing' is 167.6 cm^3 at 12 mm depth (83.8 at the 6 mm of the STL)
No out-of-plane, torsion or quantified creep check (my weak-axis check: SF 12.7 at 6 mm with 20% sideways load, so not limiting, but unstated)
Mass model assumes 2 perimeters while the owner step prescribes 3; '100 g per hanger' vs the model's 83 g; HUB_R unused; hanger-fit's 1.6 mm error hard-coded as a string

Novelty: parametric and two-piece printable hangers are common on Printables and Thingiverse and the findings are textbook beam scaling; no prior work is cited and the project is a milestone by-product, not a step to a paper

verdict: A small, clean, honest-in-its-limits engineering by-product. Every strength number I recomputed by hand (SF 48.32 for the 22 cm rack arm, 0.023 mm deflection, wire-like SF 0.13 needing 278 mm depth) and every committed STL (closed, 6 mm deep, 236-358 mm footprints) checks out. It misses the bar on claims and verification and on the median: the deliverable STL files cannot be printed on the 220 mm bed the owner steps name (w22 needs 318 mm and no split exists), the bed search is on a 5-degree grid and ignores the post, the headline says 'Yes' to an untested physical question, and four of six seeded bugs survive the 11 tests. As research it is not new: textbook beam scaling and a trivially oversize part, with no prior work cited.
